papers.title: Language performance across different progressive supranuclear palsy clinical variants.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Language abnormalities are a defining feature of the speech and language variant of progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP-SL). However, language impairments across the other clinical variants of PSP are less well understood. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate language abnormalities in PSP-Richardson's syndrome (PSP-RS), PSP predominant parkinsonism (PSP-P) and PSP progressive gait freezing (PSP-PGF) compared to PSP-SL and assess relationships with cognitive and communicative function, and neuroimaging. METHODS: One hundred eight participants (20 PSP-SL, 38 PSP-RS, 17 PSP-P, 11 PSP-PGF, 13 other PSP variants) participated. All underwent a communication evaluation including the Western Aphasia Battery (WAB). A speech-language pathologist judged presence of aphasia. The 79 patients without PSP-SL were divided based on normal versus abnormal WAB aphasia quotient (WAB-AQ). Relationships to disease severity and grey and white matter volume loss were assessed. RESULTS: Excluding PSP-SL patients, 18 patients (23%) had abnormal WAB-AQ. Lower WAB-AQ was related to worse disease severity, general cognition, working memory, and executive impairment. Only seven patients were clinically judged to have aphasia (each mild), with impairments noted in naming and grammatical comprehension. Voxel-level MRI analyses showed no differences in patterns of volume between those who had normal versus abnormal WAB-AQ. CONCLUSIONS: Abnormal WAB-AQ was observed in 23% of patients with PSP diagnosed with non-speech-language variants of PSP; however, this may overestimate aphasia as diagnosed by a speech-language pathologist (less than 10%). Performance may reflect more widespread cognitive impairment rather than primary focal language network degeneration.

One-Spin endpoint QuIC detects elevated α-synuclein amplification-associated signals in plasma EV-enriched fractions from Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) assays enable sensitive detection of misfolded α-synuclein seeds in biological samples. However, their application to plasma remains challenging because of matrix complexity and assay variability. OBJECTIVES: To evaluate a simplified plasma-based endpoint quaking-induced conversion (QuIC) workflow, termed One-Spin endpoint QuIC, for detecting α-synuclein amplification-associated signals in Parkinson's disease (PD). METHODS: One-Spin endpoint QuIC was applied to EV-enriched plasma fractions from 47 patients with PD, 10 patients with multiple system atrophy (MSA), and 30 healthy controls (HC). Group differences, exploratory diagnostic performance, and associations with clinical measures were evaluated. Amplification products were further characterized by cryo-electron microscopy. RESULTS: PD samples exhibited significantly higher endpoint thioflavin T (ThT) fluorescence than HC and MSA samples. Exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses yielded areas under the curve of 0.7397 for PD versus HC and 0.8128 for PD versus MSA. Cryo-electron microscopy revealed heterogeneous filament architectures in amplification products from EV-enriched plasma fractions, including conformations not observed in the control reactions. Filament architectures overlapped across diagnostic groups, without evidence of disease-specific structural signatures. CONCLUSIONS: One-Spin endpoint QuIC provides a simplified approach for detecting α-synuclein amplification-associated signals in plasma EV-enriched fractions. Further validation in independent cohorts is required to determine its potential utility for blood-based biomarker development in PD and related synucleinopathies.

papers.title: Treatment persistence according to the timing of safinamide initiation after motor fluctuation onset in Parkinson's disease: a retrospective real-world study.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: We examined whether safinamide treatment persistence differed according to timing of initiation after motor fluctuation onset in Parkinson's disease (PD). METHODS: We retrospectively evaluated 200 patients with PD treated with safinamide at two Italian movement disorder centers between 2016 and 2025. Turin (n = 151) was the primary cohort, while Rome (n = 49) provided supportive data for an exploratory comparison of early initiators. Early initiators started safinamide within 2 years of motor fluctuation onset; late initiators started treatment more than 2 years after onset. Treatment persistence, defined as time to permanent all-cause discontinuation, was analyzed using Kaplan-Meier methods and multivariable Cox models adjusted for age, Hoehn and Yahr stage, levodopa equivalent daily dose, and disease duration at motor fluctuation onset. RESULTS: In Turin, 95 patients were early and 56 late initiators, with 71 discontinuations. Median persistence was 94 versus 34 months (log-rank p = 0.004). Early-initiator status remained associated with a lower discontinuation hazard after adjustment (HR 0.348, 95% CI 0.198-0.611; p < 0.001) and after excluding patients receiving device-aided therapies (HR 0.302, 95% CI 0.154-0.591; p < 0.001). Each additional year between fluctuation onset and safinamide initiation was associated with a higher discontinuation hazard (HR 1.104, 95% CI 1.034-1.179; p = 0.003). Among early initiators, persistence did not differ between centers, although follow-up was shorter in Rome. CONCLUSION: Earlier safinamide initiation was associated with longer treatment persistence. This association may partly reflect differences in disease and treatment stage rather than timing itself, and prospective confirmation is needed.

papers.title: A state-of-the-art polygenic score for idiopathic Parkinson's disease: benchmarking methods and impact on genetic PD carriers.
papers.abstract: Genetic causes are identified in up to 15% of Parkinson's disease (PD) patients; the remaining idiopathic PD (iPD) patients are attributed to polygenic risk, environmental and lifestyle factors, and interactions thereof. We applied five advanced polygenic score (PGS) tools to data from 1762 iPD patients and 4227 healthy controls of European ancestry. 5-fold cross-validation revealed a significant boost in the discriminative power of modern Bayesian methods over simpler approaches, leading to the development of a novel iPD-PGS. This score demonstrated significantly improved performance compared to existing scores, achieving an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.680 (95% confidence interval (-CI):[0.665, 0.695]). External validation confirmed its robustness. Early-onset iPD patients exhibited higher PGS values than late-onset iPD patients and healthy controls, indicating increased polygenetic burden. Applying our novel iPD-PGS to carriers of heterozygous PRKN variants and GBA1 coding risk variants suggested that penetrance in these groups is partly explained by the same polygenic alterations as observed mitigating iPD. GBA1 showed a trend toward higher discriminative potential than PRKN (GBA1: AUC = 0.639, 95%-CI:[0.590, 0.687]; PRKN: AUC = 0.594, 95%-CI:[0.501, 0.687]), though confidence intervals overlapped. Our study highlights the potential of advanced PGSs in PD research, particularly in identifying high-risk individuals and modifying risk in rare-variant carriers.

papers.title: Identification of Type 1 and Type 2 α-Synuclein-Seeds by CSF Seed Amplification Assay in Patients With Movement Disorders.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: A novel α-synuclein (syn) seed amplification assay (synSAA) differentiates 2 types of syn-seeds in CSF: type1, associated with Lewy bodies (LBs), and type2, associated with glial-cytoplasmic inclusions, the hallmark of multiple system atrophy (MSA). However, syn-copathology extends beyond synucleinopathies, and copathologies are increasingly relevant. Different syn-seeds have been assessed in highly characterized research cohorts, but data assessing type and frequency in patients from routine clinical encounters are lacking. Hence, our objective was to determine frequency, type, and clinical association of different syn-seeds in CSF in a large cohort from a movement disorders (MDs) clinic. METHODS: This cross-sectional study included consecutive patients from a MD clinic between 2009 and 2025. CSF was tested with synSAA and clinical data derived from medical records. RESULTS: We recruited 1,059 patients (mean age 70.5 ± 10.5 years; 38.4% female; mean disease duration 4.0 ± 4.6 years). Syn-seeds were detected in 54.2% of patients, with type1-seeds predominating (88.5%). High synSAA positivity was observed in Parkinson disease (PD) (84.7%), dementia with LB (93.4%), MSA (84.5%), isolated REM-sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) (80.0%), and normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) with PD (87.0%). Undetermined hypokinetic MD showed 53.7% positivity. Moderate proportions (∼25-33%) were detected in Alzheimer disease, progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP), corticobasal syndrome, and idiopathic NPH without PD, while other neurologic disorders showed 20.9% positivity. Type2-seeds were the major seed type in MSA (79.6% of syn-seeds) and minor type in PD (6.2%), PSP (9.1%), and undetermined hypokinetic MD (13.8%). Overall, type2-seeds were present in only 2.6% of non-MSA patients. Patients with type1-seeds had worse olfaction and more hallucinations. papers.title: The Burden of Neurologic Disorders in Canada, 1990-2023: A Systematic Analysis in the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Neurologic disorders are leading contributors to global disability and mortality, yet Canada-specific burden estimates have not been updated with the most recent Global Burden of Disease (GBD) data. We aimed to quantify the burden of 18 neurologic conditions in Canada in 2023, characterize trends from 1990 to 2023, describe age-specific and sex-specific patterns, and compare Canada with the high-income country average. METHODS: This retrospective epidemiologic modeling study analyzed GBD 2023 data for Canada. Eighteen conditions whose primary health loss manifestation directly affects the central or peripheral nervous system were included. Outcome measures included prevalence, mortality, and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) comprising years lived with disability (YLDs) and years of life lost (YLL). Age-standardized rates are all per 100,000 population. 95% uncertainty intervals (UI) are reported for all estimates. RESULTS: Modeling evaluated the entire Canadian population across 34 years. In 2023, neurologic disorders accounted for 11.48% (UI: 9.47-14.26) of total DALYs and 16.31% (UI: 10.56-26.24) of deaths. Burden was heavily driven by nonfatal disability metrics (YLDs); Alzheimer disease and other dementias led absolute DALYs at 366,548.5 (UI: 180,491.8-710,281.4), followed by migraine at 232,619.5 (UI: 151,390.4-320,391.1) and ischemic stroke at 223,748.0 (UI: 194,981.3-249,309.6). Migraine led age-standardized DALY rates at 565.8 (UI: 374.0-783.1) per 100,000, driven entirely by nonfatal disability metrics. Dementias drove mortality with 20,108.6 (UI: 4,999.6-50,266.6) deaths. From 1990 to 2023, the steepest age-standardized DALY rate increases occurred in other neurologic disorders (153.6% [UI: 129.0-185.1]), encephalitis (59.2% [UI: 25.1-95.6]), and Parkinson disease (25.4% [UI: 18.9-33.0]), while meningitis declined by 62.6% (UI: 57.4-66.9). papers.title: Agent Orange Exposure and Diagnosis of Parkinson Disease and Related Disorders Among US Veterans.
papers.abstract: IMPORTANCE: The risk of Parkinson disease (PD) due to Agent Orange, the Vietnam War Era defoliant, is inferred from studies of agricultural pesticide exposure. Epidemiological work is currently lacking. OBJECTIVE: To examine the association between Agent Orange exposure with incident cases of synucleinopathies including Parkinson disease, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) among US veterans. DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This was an electronic health record-based cohort study inclusive of medical records from January 1, 1999, to December 30, 2022. Veterans were followed up for a mean (SD) of 12.5 (7.0) years from the start of records. Analyses were conducted from July 2024 to July 2026. The setting was the US Department of Veterans Affairs and included US veterans who served during the Vietnam War Era (August 1964 to May 1975) were screened. Those with incomplete demographic data or prevalent synucleinopathies before or within 6 months of follow-up were excluded. EXPOSURE: Agent Orange defined by self-report. Direct or occupational exposure was defined by involvement in Operation Ranch Hand, Army Chemical Corps, and/or direct handling or spraying. MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Cumulative incidence of synucleinopathies was calculated adjusting for competing risk of death, age, traumatic brain injury, and frailty. RESULTS: After screening of 4 917 272 US veterans, 4 468 509 veterans (mean [SD] age, 60.6 [8] years; 4 380 139 male [98%]) were included in analyses. A total of 1 035 210 veterans (23.2%) had Agent Orange exposure; 7600 (0.2%) of these had direct or occupational exposure. papers.title: Agent Orange and Parkinson Disease-The War Ended, the Exposure Did Not.
Risk factors for early-onset Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Prospective evidence on factors associated with early-onset Parkinson's disease (EOPD) remains limited. We aimed to identify factors associated with incident EOPD and compare their associations with late-onset Parkinson's disease (LOPD). METHODS: This prospective cohort study included 283,934 participants aged <60 years and free of Parkinson's disease at baseline. Thirty-eight prespecified factors were evaluated using Cox regression with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction, followed by an exploratory mutually adjusted analysis. Sex-stratified and EOPD-LOPD comparative analyses were conducted, and sensitivity analyses excluded EOPD events occurring within the first 2 or 5 years of follow-up. RESULTS: During 2,298,992 person-years of follow-up, 168 participants developed EOPD. After mutual adjustment, EOPD was associated with older age [hazard ratio (HR) per year, 1.15; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.10-1.20], male sex (HR, 1.93; 95% CI, 1.41-2.64), a higher polygenic risk score (HR per unit, 1.53; 95% CI, 1.31-1.78), family history of Parkinson's disease (HR, 4.03; 95% CI, 2.49-6.50), anxiety (HR, 2.48; 95% CI, 1.60-3.86), constipation (HR, 4.90; 95% CI, 3.31-7.25), and autoimmune disease burden (HR per category, 1.98; 95% CI, 1.32-2.96). Associations with handgrip strength, hypertension, and migraine were attenuated after mutual adjustment. The principal associations were broadly consistent after excluding EOPD events occurring within the first 2 and 5 years of follow-up. Interaction tests suggested stronger associations of family history, constipation, and autoimmune disease burden with EOPD than with LOPD. CONCLUSION: EOPD showed a distinct profile of associated risk factors, particularly greater autoimmune disease burden and familial susceptibility. These findings support heterogeneity in Parkinson's disease according to age at onset.

papers.title: Normative references of corpus callosum across lifespan and application in neurological and neuroimmunological disorders.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The corpus callosum (CC) is the largest white matter structure and is often affected in neurological and neuroimmunological disorders. However, previous studies mainly used group-level comparisons. This limits patient-level magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) assessment. Exploratory clinical analyses suggest potential applications that require further validation.

papers.title: Magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS)- thalamotomy for Parkinson's disease: clinical outcomes and exploratory lesion analysis.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The efficacy of magnetic resonance-guided focused ultrasound (MRgFUS)-thalamotomy for treating drug-resistant tremor in patients with Parkinson's disease (PD) remains insufficiently understood. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate clinical outcomes and their relationship with lesion characteristics in such patients treated with MRgFUS-thalamotomy. METHODS: 74 patients were included, with 60, 42, 45, and 17 evaluated at 1, 3, 6, and 12 months post-treatment, respectively. Changes in total MDS-UPDRS III tremor score, as well as resting, postural, and action tremor in the treated hand, resting tremor in the treated leg, and the frequency and severity of adverse events (AEs), were assessed at 6 months. In 34 patients, correlations between tremor improvement at 6 months and lesion volume and location on MRI (30 min and 6 months post-treatment) were analyzed. RESULTS: Hand (total, resting, postural, and action) and leg tremor scores improved significantly at all time points (p < 0.001), with more than 70% improvement at 6 months. AEs were reported in 71%, 39%, and 27% of patients at 1, 3, and 6 months, respectively, and were mostly mild and transient. Five patients experienced moderate AEs, most resolving by 6 months, and one patient had a severe AE. A greater lesion overlap with the VLpv at 6 months, as well as larger, more anterior and dorsal lesions at 30 min post-treatment, was associated with greater improvement in resting hand and leg tremor. CONCLUSION: MRgFUS-thalamotomy significantly improves hand and leg tremor in drug-resistant PD tremor, with an acceptable safety profile. Lesion location appears to influence treatment efficacy.

papers.title: Integrative transcriptomic and machine learning analyses identify NOL7 and TXLNA as candidate blood biomarkers for Parkinson's disease within an RNA modification-associated co-expression network.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Parkinson's disease (PD) pathogenesis involves complex molecular mechanisms, with emerging evidence implicating RNA modifications (RM). This study sought to explore RM-associated key genes and their roles in PD progression. METHODS: Transcriptomic datasets GSE6613 (training) and GSE72267 (validation) were analyzed. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between PD and controls were recognized. WGCNA was performed to identify RM-associated module genes. Machine learning algorithms, Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) analysis, and gene expression validation were applied to screen key genes. Nomogram construction, functional enrichment, immune infiltration analysis were conducted to investigate the biological mechanisms and therapeutic potential of the key genes. The bioinformatics findings were further supported by RT-qPCR experiments in a small clinical cohort (n = 5 per group), though these preliminary results require validation in larger independent samples. RESULTS: Through intersection of 507 DEGs and 2,091 RM-associated module genes, 63 candidate genes related to RM in PD were identified. Machine learning, ROC analysis, gene expression validation, and clinical experiments were further employed to identify two key genes (NOL7 and TXLNA). A nomogram constructed based on key genes demonstrated moderate diagnostic efficacy for PD, with an area under the curve of 0.792. Enrichment analyses revealed associations of the key genes with neuroactive pathways, such as spliceosome and ribosome. Immune infiltration analysis suggested a negative correlation between NOL7 and NKT (cor = -0.30, P < 0.05). Furthermore, danazol was predicted to be a compound associated with both NOL7 and TXLNA. Molecular docking analysis revealed that danazol exhibited a relatively favorable binding affinity for NOL7 (-6.3 kcal/mol), whereas its binding affinity for TXLNA was weaker (-4.7 kcal/mol). papers.title: Taurine metabolism: a potential target for neuroprotection in age-related neurodegenerative diseases.
papers.journal: Mammalian genome : official journal of the International Mammalian Genome Society
papers.abstract: Taurine is one of the most abundant free amino acids in mammals and plays essential roles in cellular homeostasis, mitochondrial function, calcium regulation and neuronal survival. Taurine availability varies markedly across tissues, species and sexes, reflecting the balance between endogenous synthesis, dietary intake, transport and efflux. Although reduced taurine levels have been reported in some aging tissues, recent longitudinal studies indicate that circulating taurine does not decline universally with age, and its value as a biomarker of aging remains debated. Alterations in taurine or its transporter SLC6A6 have been described in Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis, Huntington's disease and retinal degenerations. Preclinical studies indicate that taurine supplementation mitigates excitotoxicity, stabilizes mitochondrial function, reduces neuroinflammation and supports myelination and synaptic balance. Despite this strong mechanistic rationale, clinical evidence remains limited and heterogeneous, underscoring the need for biomarker-guided trials and a clearer definition of optimal therapeutic windows. In this review, we summarize the general properties of taurine and its metabolic regulation. We examine taurine's neuroprotective properties across different neurodegenerative conditions and discuss future perspectives for targeting taurine metabolism as a promising but largely unexplored strategy for intervention in age-related neurodegenerative diseases.

papers.title: Corneal nerve status as a biomarker for neurodegenerative and neurological diseases: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Corneal nerve status has gained prominence as a potential adjunctive biomarker for neurodegenerative and neurological diseases, as corneal small-fibre abnormalities can be detected in peripheral neuropathy and may precede conventional manifestations in certain conditions. Advances in in vivo confocal microscopy (IVCM) allow non-invasive, cellular-level assessments of corneal nerve alterations in real-time. Corneal nerve metrics have been associated with disease progression and severity. This review explores the role of corneal nerve status in the evaluation and monitoring of neurodegenerative and neurological diseases or conditions, including diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN), Parkinson's disease (PD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia, multiple sclerosis (MS), schizophrenia, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), migraine, tauopathies, and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP). The strength and maturity of evidence vary substantially between conditions. DPN has the most established evidence base, with replicated cross-sectional and longitudinal studies showing reductions in corneal nerve fibre density, branch density and length, and evidence that corneal nerve loss may precede conventional manifestations of neuropathy. In MS, longitudinal studies demonstrate progressive corneal nerve loss associated with worsening disability. In PD, the extent of corneal nerve fibre loss correlates with severity of motor deterioration, cognitive impairment and development of autonomic dysfunction, although proposed applications in prodromal detection, disease phenotyping, and prognostication remain largely dependent on small, single-centre studies. Studies in MCI and dementia suggest potential diagnostic and prognostic utility, including comparisons with neuroimaging, but are largely derived from overlapping single-centre cohorts. papers.title: The role of immune-related transcription factors as a therapeutic approach to Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Therapeutic modulation of immune-related transcription factors (TFs) in Parkinson's disease (PD) is an emerging approach aimed at remodeling immune and inflammatory gene expression that may contribute to disease onset and progression. PD is a neurodegenerative disorder defined by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra of the brain due to the aggregation of misfolded α-synuclein into Lewy bodies. PD presents with various motor symptoms, such as tremors, rigidity, and bradykinesia, alongside significant non-motor symptoms, including cognitive decline and mood disorders. Levodopa, a dopamine precursor, is the most commonly used drug to treat PD. It can improve movement problems associated with PD but does not provide a definitive cure. Recent findings have highlighted TFs and their interactions with multiple signaling pathways with regard to neuronal survival and function. Notably, the dysregulation of immune responses and chronic inflammation have been implicated in PD's pathophysiology, highlighting the importance of targeting TFs that regulate these processes. TFs are crucial regulators of gene expression, influencing various immune processes by binding to specific DNA sequences in gene promoter and enhancer regions. The modulation of TFs offers potential avenues for treating conditions characterized by immune dysregulation, such as PD. Investigating the immune system is intriguing as it opens new windows into the disease mechanisms and potential targets for intervention. Despite the potential benefits of targeting these TFs, challenges remain in translating preclinical findings into clinical practice, including the delivery of therapies, the risk of off-target effects, and the variability in patient responses. As research continues to unveil the intricate roles of immune-related TFs, novel therapeutic approaches could enhance outcomes for individuals with PD, representing a vital area of ongoing exploration in PD research.

papers.title: Gut microbial metabolites: linking gut-immune-brain crosstalk to mental and neuropsychiatric health.
papers.abstract: This narrative review adopts the gut-immune-brain axis as the core framework. Literature published 2010-2025 was retrieved from PubMed, Web of Science and ScienceDirect; landmark pre-2010 studies from top journals were also included. Literature was analyzed across five dimensions: metabolite synthesis-transport, intestinal immune regulation, central mediation, disease-pathology links and clinical translation. We elucidate how short-chain fatty acids, tryptophan metabolites and bile acids act as immune messengers to modulate neural homeostasis. Under physiological conditions, they maintain barrier integrity and central immune balance; when dysregulated, they trigger immune disturbance, blood-brain barrier damage and neuroinflammation, promoting Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, major depressive disorder and chronic insomnia. Moving beyond conventional gut-brain-axis reviews focused merely on gut-brain communication, this work highlights immunity as the critical intermediate node and constructs the cascade "gut microbial metabolites-immune regulation-neural homeostasis-disease". We further summarize biomarker prospects and intervention strategies including dietary fiber, pre-/probiotics and fecal microbiota transplantation. Notably, an ICH-M10-aligned five-stage biomarker validation framework and a gut-brain-immune tri-culture microfluidic model are proposed, offering new directions for mechanistic research and precision therapy for neurological disorders.

papers.title: Baicalein and Baicalein-loaded liposomes attenuate manganese-induced injury in the rat substantia nigra.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVES: Manganese (Mn) can accumulate in the brain, damage the basal ganglia and cause Parkinsonian phenotypes. Baicalein (BA), a natural flavonoid, shows therapeutic promise driven by its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties. This study aimed to evaluate whether BA and baicalein-loaded liposomes (BA-LPs) reduce Mn-induced injury to the substantia nigra. METHODS: Sixty male Wistar rats were allocated into six groups: control, Mn (50 mg/kg), BA (30 mg/kg), BA-LPs, and Mn combined with either BA or BA-LPs. Treatments were administered intraperitoneally twice weekly for four weeks, with BA and BA-LP pretreatments one hour before Mn exposure. Markers of oxidative stress and antioxidant defence, glial and astrocyte presence, neuroinflammation, apoptosis, histopathological and ultrastructural damage, and tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) and dopamine levels in the substantia nigra were assessed. RESULTS: Mn exposure significantly disrupted redox homeostasis, evidenced by significantly reduced Nrf2, HO-1, SOD, CAT, and GPx expression and protein activities, and elevated malondialdehyde levels. Mn exposure increased microglial and astrocytic biomarkers, as shown by elevated Iba-1 and GFAP, and induced neuroinflammation with elevated TLR4, NF-κB, IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α, NO, and iNOS expression and protein activities. Mn increased levels of caspases 3 and 8 and a Bax/Bcl-2 ratio indicative of elevated apoptosis. Mn treatment caused histopathological and ultrastructural damage, and reduced TH and dopamine levels. In the Mn + BA and Mn + BA-LPs co-treatments, markers of antioxidant defences were significantly restored, neuroinflammation reduced, apoptosis attenuated, and TH and dopamine levels partially restored. Histological and ultrastructural findings confirmed reduced cellular damage in neuronal tissue with BA and BA-LPs co-treatments. papers.title: Speech and Language Abnormalities in Putative Brain-First Versus Body-First Parkinson's Disease.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: The α-synuclein origin model proposes brain-first and body-first Parkinson's disease (PD) subtypes, with speech potentially revealing their distinct neurodegenerative patterns. OBJECTIVE: We aimed to analyze the possible speech and language differences between untreated PD patients with premotor (putative body-first) and without (putative brain-first) rapid eye movement sleep behavior disorder. METHODS: Speech samples of reading passages and monologues were automatically analyzed using acoustic and linguistic features. RESULTS: We enrolled 23 body-first and 35 brain-first de novo PD patients compared with 35 healthy controls. Brain-first patients showed greater speech impairment severity compared with body-first patients (P = 0.002) and controls (P < 0.001), whereas body-first patients showed greater language impairment severity compared with brain-first patients (P < 0.001) and controls (P < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: Putative brain-first subtype had more motor speech abnormalities whereas body-first subtype manifested greater language impairment. Thes finding is consistent with motor-dominant nigrostriatal involvement in brain-first and broader non-motor/cognitive involvement in body-first PD. © 2026 The Author(s). papers.title: Effectiveness and Safety of Cannabis on Anxiety Treatment Outcomes: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: We assessed controlled non-interventional studies and randomized clinical trials (RCTs) evaluating THC-containing cannabis' safety and effectiveness for anxiety. METHODS: We searched PubMed, Embase, APA PsychInfo, and Cochrane databases in February 2023 for clinical studies that reported patient-level controlled quantitative assessments of anxiety outcomes following cannabis treatment. Exclusion criteria included: publication before 2000, in non-English language, assessment of topical treatment or containing <0.3% tetrahydrocannabinol, and FDA-approved products. We assessed risk of bias via RoB2/ROBINS-I, and rated evidence quality using the GRADE approach. PROSPERO:CRD42023411999. RESULTS: From 6,453 search records, 4 RCTs and 1 observational study met inclusion criteria. All studies involved patients with severe comorbid medical conditions, with anxiety assessed as a secondary outcome, limiting generalizability to primary anxiety disorders. Interventions included THC-rich cannabis oil for fibromyalgia, cannabinoids for obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), cannabidiol (CBD)-enriched extracts for Parkinson's disease, nabiximols (THC:CBD 1:1) for multiple sclerosis (MS), and cannabis for chronic non-cancer pain. Anxiety was measured via self-reported scales. Due to heterogeneity in anxiety measures, results were synthesized narratively. Compared with placebo, the OCD RCT showed significant anxiety worsening [4.31 (1.70, 6.92)]; the Parkinson's disease RCT non-significant improvement [-0.82 (-1.97, 0.33)], and the fibromyalgia and MS RCTs show no significant effects [0.38 (-2.91, 3.67); -2.00 (-7.51, 3.51)]. The pain observational study reported no initial significant effect on anxiety -0.30 (-1.53, 0.93). Quality of life (QoL) worsened with THC in Parkinson's [-0.14 (-0.23, -0.04)] and showed non-significant improvement in MS [0.35 (-1.09, 1.79)]. The evidence quality was rated low to moderate. papers.title: Health-Related Quality of Life Across Neurologic Conditions: A Cross-Sectional Cohort Study Using Real-World Patient-Reported Outcomes.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Health-related quality of life (HRQOL) is an important outcome within value-based care for patients with neurologic conditions. The American Academy of Neurology recommends the use of Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS) Global Health as a patient-reported outcome performance measure to assess stability or improvement over 1 year. However, interpretation of this measure requires an understanding of HRQOL across neurologic populations. Our study leveraged real-world data collected through the electronic health record to characterize differences in HRQOL across common neurologic conditions. papers.title: Non-pharmacological fatigue management strategies in neurodegenerative conditions: a scoping review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Fatigue is a common and disabling symptom across several neurodegenerative diseases, including multiple sclerosis and Parkinson's disease. Non-pharmacological strategies are widely used in clinical practice to address fatigue, yet the extent to which evidence from one neurodegenerative condition can inform fatigue management in others remains uncertain, particularly for Parkinson's disease where intervention trials are scarce. OBJECTIVES: To map the quantitative evidence on non-pharmacological interventions for fatigue in adults with neurodegenerative diseases (excluding dementias), and to identify potentially transferable strategies, gaps, and priorities for research and practice, with particular relevance to Parkinson's disease. DESIGN: Scoping review conducted according to Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported using the PRISMA Extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). The protocol was preregistered on the Open Science Framework (OSF; DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/MJEYP). DATA SOURCES: MEDLINE, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, AMED, and PsycINFO were searched for records published from January 2006 to 15 February 2025. Reference lists of relevant reviews and included studies were screened. Publications in English or Arabic were eligible. ELIGIBILITY CRITERIA: Quantitative interventional studies, mixed-methods studies with extractable quantitative fatigue outcomes, and systematic reviews/meta-analyses evaluating non-pharmacological interventions for fatigue in adults with progressive neurodegenerative conditions were eligible. Conditions of interest included multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's disease, motor neurone disease, Huntington's disease, hereditary ataxias, multiple system atrophy, and progressive supranuclear palsy. Studies focusing solely on pharmacological, surgical, herbal, or homeopathic interventions, qualitative-only studies, and studies in dementias were excluded. papers.title: Denial of Hardware-Related Skin Erosion in Patients with Effective Deep Brain Stimulation: A Novel Phenomenon.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is an established therapy that can significantly improve patients' quality of life in several disorders. Besides its benefits, hardware-related problems including erosion and wound infections are well known problems. In the present series, we describe a novel phenomenon manifesting as denial for hardware-related skin erosion in patients with movement disorders benefiting from DBS in various targets. METHODS: Patients were collected from two large DBS cohorts over a period of 28 years. The skin erosion was identified upon the occasion of a routine follow-up with the patients apparently being unaware/not noticing its occurrence. Demographic, clinical, and operative data were analyzed. Additionally, the hardware-related skin erosion and its time of diagnosis, as well as the consecutive treatment, were registered. RESULTS: Overall, 5 patients were identified with denial for hardware-related skin erosion. Three were men; two were women. The mean age at surgery was 66 years (range, 54-78). Three patients had dystonia; 2 patients had Parkinson's disease. DBS targets were the globus pallidus internus and various thalamic nuclei. All patients benefited markedly from chronic DBS (mean improvement of 76.7% according to the specific rating scales). The hardware-related skin erosion was diagnosed at a median follow-up of 18 months after DBS implantation (range, 5-264 months). Despite multiple surgical attempts at preservation, the neurostimulation system was ultimately explanted in 3 patients. CONCLUSION: Denial toward hardware-related skin erosion in DBS, most probably denial, is a rare but potentially serious complication during chronic DBS.

papers.title: Historical Perspectives on Spinocerebellar Ataxia Type 2: The Cuban Contribution.
papers.journal: Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society
papers.abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 2 (SCA2) is one of the most extensively investigated hereditary ataxias worldwide. Although the first clinical description of the disorder was reported in India in 1971 by Wadia and Swami, the province of Holguín, Cuba subsequently became recognized as a major geographical focus of SCA2, with a particularly high concentration of affected families and individuals, where it became internationally recognized as Cuban ataxia. Since the late 1970s, Cuban investigators have played a pivotal role in the clinical, epidemiological, neuropathological, and genetic characterization of the disorder. This article presents a historical review of the scientific development of Cuban ataxia based on a comprehensive bibliographic and documentary analysis, complemented by interviews with key neurologists involved in its early investigation. Particular emphasis is placed on the pioneering contributions of José Rafael Estrada González, Lionel Valles Calaña, Guillermo Orozco Díaz, and Luis Velázquez Pérez, whose work established the foundations for the current understanding of SCA2. Their investigations culminated in the identification of one of the world's largest SCA2 clusters and substantially advanced knowledge of the disease's clinical spectrum, epidemiology, and molecular genetics. The Cuban experience illustrates how sustained clinical observation, multidisciplinary collaboration, and international partnerships transformed a regional neurological disorder into one of the best-characterized hereditary ataxias worldwide. © 2026 International Parkinson and Movement Disorder Society.
